props.title: Poison

sections.content: Todd Haynes's provocative **Poison (1991)** (1991) revolutionized New Queer Cinema alongside films like **Paris is Burning** (1990) and **My Own Private Idaho** (1991). Using three intercut narratives - a mock documentary about a flying boy, a 1950s B-movie horror story, and a homoerotic prison tale based on Jean Genet - Haynes crafted a bold statement about societal outcasts and moral panic. The film sparked controversy when it received NEA funding, becoming a lightning rod in the culture wars while earning praise at Sundance.

sections.content: **Poison** emerged from the same fertile NYC underground scene that produced directors like Jim Jarmusch and Hal Hartley. Its experimental structure and unflinching queer content challenged mainstream conventions while building on the transgressive work of Kenneth Anger in films like **Scorpio Rising** (1964). The AIDS crisis loomed large over the film's reception, with its themes of contamination and stigma speaking directly to the epidemic's impact on the gay community.

Haynes's use of different film genres - documentary, horror, prison drama - creates a kaleidoscopic view of how society creates and punishes its "others." This technique influenced later multi-narrative films like **Three Colors: Blue** (1993) and **Pulp Fiction** (1994), while its frank sexuality paved the way for works like **Hedwig and the Angry Inch** (2001). SUBHEAD: Impact on Independent Cinema

movies.title: Far From Heaven

sections.content: The success of **Poison** at Sundance helped establish a new model for independent film distribution through companies like Fine Line Features. Its bold mixing of styles influenced directors like Derek Jarman (**Edward II**, 1991) and Gregg Araki (**The Living End**, 1992), while its political engagement through formal experimentation echoes in contemporary work like **Moonlight** (2016).
